translations.text: There was a man from Ramathaim, from Siphah in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Elkanah. He was the son of Jerahmeel, the son of Elijah, the son of Toke, in Asib in the hill country of Ephraim.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.

The man used to go up from his city, Ramathaim, day after day to worship and offer sacrifices [?] to the Lord God of hosts at Shiloh. Eli the priest was there with his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who served as priests of the Lord.
When the appointed day came, Elkanah slaughtered his sacrifice and gave portions to Peninnah his wife, and to all his sons and daughters.
To Hannah herself he gave just one portion, for her alone, because she had no children. But Elkanah loved Hannah more than Peninnah, and the Lord had closed off her womb.

For the Lord himself had not given her children, in keeping with her affliction and the discouragement she felt in her affliction. She was distressed and discouraged because of this, because the Lord had closed off her womb and had not given her children.
This was how she acted every year when she went up to the house of the Lord. She was sorrowful and wept, and would not sit down to eat.

Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah!” She said to him, “Here I am, my lord. I am listening to you.” He said to her, “Why are you crying like this? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart troubled? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
She rose after they had eaten at Shiloh and stood before the Lord. Eli the priest was sitting on the [?] at the gates of the Lord’s temple.
She was deeply discouraged and prayed to the Lord, speaking through her tears.

She made a vow to the Lord, saying, “Adonai, Lord, my God of hosts, if you will truly look upon the humiliation of your servant, remember me, and give your servant a male child, I will give him to you to honor you in your presence until the day of his death. He will drink neither wine nor strong drink, and no razor will touch his head.”
As she continued praying before the Lord, Eli the priest watched her mouth.
She was speaking in her heart, and her lips were moving, but her voice could not be heard. Eli thought she was drunk.
The son of Eli said to her, “How long will you remain drunk? Get rid of your wine and stop this here before the Lord.”
Hannah answered, “I am not drunk, my lord. I am a woman whose heart is troubled today. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I am pouring out my soul before the Lord.”
“Do not regard your servant as an outcast woman, for it is because I have so much to say that I have continued until now.”
Eli answered her, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant you your whole request, which you have asked of him.”
She said to him, “Your servant has found favor in your eyes.” The woman went on her way, entered her lodging, sat down, and ate with her husband. She drank, and her face was no longer sad.

They rose early in the morning, bowed down, worshiped the Lord, and went on their way. Elkanah returned to his house in Ramathaim and had intercourse with Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her.
She drank. And when the time came, she gave birth to a son and named him Samuel, saying, “I asked the Lord of hosts for him.”
The man Elkanah went up with his whole household to Shiloh to slaughter the annual sacrifice and to give his tithes and all the tithes of his land.
But Hannah did not go up with him, because she had said to her husband, “I will stay until the little boy grows strong and I wean him. Then he will appear before the Lord and remain there forever.”

Elkanah her husband said to her, “Do what is good in your eyes. Stay until you wean the little boy. May the Lord fulfill what has come from your mouth.” So the woman stayed and nursed her son until she weaned him.

She went up with him to Shiloh, taking a three-year-old calf, some bread, a measure of fine flour, and a measure of wine. She entered the house of the Lord at Shiloh, with the little boy accompanying them.

They presented him before the Lord. His father slaughtered the sacrifice that he regularly offered [?] the Lord at the appointed time. He brought the little boy and slaughtered the calf. Hannah, the little boy’s mother, approached Eli.
She said to him, “As you live, my lord, listen to me: I am the woman who stood here before you to pray before the Lord.”
“It was for this little child that I prayed to him, and the Lord granted me the request I made of him.”
“So I too will give him as a gift to the Lord for all the days of his life, so that he may be in the Lord’s presence.”
And immediately she said, “My heart has been strengthened in the Lord; my horn has been raised high in my God. My mouth has opened wide against my enemies. I rejoice, Lord, in your salvation.”
“For no one else is holy like the Lord, and no one else is righteous like our God. There is no other holy one besides you.”
“Do not boast, and do not speak grandly. Do not let arrogance come out of your mouths, for the Lord is the God of knowledge, and he is the God who prepares his deeds.”
“The bow of the mighty has been destroyed, and those who are weak have clothed themselves with strength.”

“Those who had their fill of bread have become needy, while those who were needy have left behind the toil of the land. For the barren woman has given birth to seven children, while the woman with many children has become weak.”
The Lord is the one who kills, and he is also the one who gives life. He brings people down to the realm of the dead and brings them up.
“The Lord is the one who gives poverty and wealth, who brings humiliation and exaltation.”
“He helps the afflicted up from the earth and raises the poor from the dung heap. He seats him with the mighty of the people, giving them a glorious throne to inherit.”
He grants the vow of the one who makes a vow and blesses the years of the righteous, for a mighty man’s strength is not his own.

“The Lord will weaken his enemy. The Lord is holy. Do not let the wise person boast in his wisdom, and do not let the mighty person boast in his might, and do not let the rich person boast in his wealth. Instead, let whoever boasts boast in the Lord, understanding the Lord and knowing him, and practicing justice and righteousness in the midst of the earth. The Lord went up into heaven and thundered. He is the one who will judge the whole earth, and he will give strength to kings and raise high the horn of his anointed one. Do not let the wise person boast in his wisdom, and do not let the mighty person boast in his might, and do not let the rich person boast in his wealth. Instead, let whoever boasts boast in the Lord, understanding the Lord and knowing him, and practicing justice and righteousness in the midst of the earth. The Lord went up into heaven and thundered. He is the one who will judge the whole earth, and he will give strength to kings and raise high the horn of his anointed one.”
They left the little boy there before the Lord and went up to Ramathaim. The young boy served before the Lord in the presence of Eli the priest.
The sons of Eli the priest were wicked sons who did not know the Lord,
nor the priest’s rightful due from the people. Whenever anyone came to offer a sacrifice, the priest’s son would come while the meat was cooking, with a three-pronged fork in his hand.

He would plunge it into the large pot, the small pot, or the cauldron, and the priest would take for himself everything that came up on the fork. This is what they did to all Israel who came to sacrifice to the Lord at Shiloh.

And before the sacrifice took place, the priest’s son would come and say to the person offering the sacrifice, “Bring meat to roast for the priest. I will not take from you what is boiled in the pot.”

The person offering the sacrifice said to him, “Let the sacrifice be carried out properly, and then take for yourself whatever you desire from all of it.” But he said to him, “I will not wait. You must give it to me now. If you do not give it, I will take it against your will.”
This deed that the priest’s sons were doing was a very, very great sin before the Lord, because they treated the Lord’s sacrifice with contempt.
But Samuel served before the Lord as a young boy, wearing an ephod.
His mother made him a little robe and brought it up to him at the appointed time, when she went up with her husband to offer the sacrifice at the appointed time.
Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife, saying to him, “May the Lord give you offspring in place of this gift that you gave to the Lord.” And Elkanah went up to his home.
The Lord visited Hannah, and she gave birth to three more sons and two more daughters. The boy Samuel served before the Lord.
Eli was very old, and he heard what his sons were doing to the Israelites: his sons were sleeping with the wives of those stationed at the entrance to the tent of testimony.
Eli said to them, “Why are you doing these things, according to this report that I hear from all the Lord’s people?
No, my sons! These reports that I hear are not good. Do not do these things, for the reports I hear are not good: you are not allowing the people to offer sacrifices to the Lord.

If someone sins against another person, people ask the Lord on his behalf to forgive him. But if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” They did not listen to their father’s voice, because God was determined to destroy them.
The boy Samuel continued to grow and was pleasing to the Lord and to people.
A man of God came to Eli and said to him, “This is what the Lord says: ‘I certainly revealed myself to your father’s household when they were in the land of Egypt, enslaved to Pharaoh’s household.

I chose your father’s household from all the tribes of Israel to be priests for me, to go up to my altar, to offer sacrifices to me, and to clothe themselves in the ephod. I gave your father’s household everything that the Israelites offer on my altar, for them to eat.
Why have you looked shamelessly at my sacrifice and my offering? You have honored your sons more than me, so that they benefit from the first portions of every sacrifice Israel offers before me.

Therefore, this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: “I said that your household and your father’s household would walk before me, serving me forever. But now,” says the Lord, “this will not happen. Those who honor me I will honor, but whoever dishonors me I will dishonor.”
Look, days are coming when I will cut off your descendants and the descendants of your father’s household,
so that there will never be an old man in my house.
I will not cut off one man from my altar, so that his eyes may fail and his soul waste away. Everyone remaining in your household will fall by the sword of men.
This will be the sign that will come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: both of them will die on the same day.
I will raise up a faithful priest for myself, who will do everything that is in my heart and in my soul. I will build him a lasting household, and he will walk before my anointed one all his days.
Whoever remains in your household will come and bow before him for a silver coin and a loaf of bread, saying, “Assign me a place of service among your priestly duties so that I may eat bread.”’”
The boy Samuel served the Lord in the presence of Eli the priest. The word of the Lord was scarce in those days, and visions were not widespread.
In those days Eli was sleeping in his place. His eyes had grown dim and heavy, and he could not see.
The lamp of God had not yet been prepared. Samuel was sleeping in the temple, in the place where the ark of God was.
The Lord called Samuel, saying, “Samuel, Samuel!” He answered, “Here I am! I have come.”
He ran to Eli and said to him, “Here I am! I have come because you called me.” Eli said to him, “I did not call you. Go and lie down.” He turned back, went away, and lay down.

The Lord called again, “Samuel, Samuel!” He ran to Eli again, for the second time, and said to him, “Here I am! I have come because you called me.” Eli said to him, “I did not call you. Go and lie down.”
Samuel did not yet know God, and the word of the Lord had not been revealed to him.

The Lord called Samuel a third time, saying, “Samuel!” He got up again and ran to Eli, saying to him, “Here I am! I have come because you are calling me.” Then Eli understood that it was the Lord who had called the boy.
Eli said to him, “Go back and lie down, my son. If he calls you, say, ‘Lord, speak; your servant is listening.’” Samuel went and lay down in his place.
And the Lord came before him and called to him as before. Samuel said, “Speak; your servant is listening to you.”
The Lord said to Samuel, “Look, I will carry out my words in Israel, so that the ears of everyone who hears them will ring.”
“On that day I will bring upon Eli everything I have spoken against his household. I will begin to carry it out and finish it.
And I told him that I myself would judge his household forever for the wrongdoing of his sons, because his sons were speaking evil against God, and he did not correct them.
And this will not happen. I swore concerning Eli’s household that the wrongdoing of Eli’s household would never be forgiven through an offering or sacrifices.”
Samuel slept until morning. He rose early in the morning and opened the doors of the Lord’s house. But Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli called out to Samuel, “Samuel, my son!” He said, “Here I am; I am listening.”
Eli said to him, “What is the message that was spoken to you? Do not hide it from me. May God act against you if you hide from me a single word of everything that was spoken in your hearing.”
And Samuel told Eli everything and hid nothing from him. Eli said, “He is the Lord. Let him do what is good in his sight.”
Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and not one of all his words fell to the ground.
And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a trustworthy prophet of God.

And the Lord continued to make himself known to them at Shiloh, for the Lord revealed himself to Samuel. Samuel was established as a prophet of the Lord to all Israel, from one end of the land to the other. Eli was very old, and his sons continued in their conduct, and their way was evil.
In those days the Philistines gathered to wage war against Israel. Israel went out to meet them in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.

And the Philistines drew up their battle line to fight Israel. The battle grew fierce against Israel, and the men of Israel were defeated before the Philistines. Four thousand men were struck down in the battle that took place in the open country.

The people returned to the camp, and the elders of Israel said to one another, “Why has the Lord humbled us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of our God from Shiloh. Let it come and remain among us and save us from the hands of our enemies.”
So the people sent to Shiloh, and they brought from there the ark of the Lord, with the cherubim upon it. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, came with the ark of the Lord.
When the ark of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel rose up, shouting with a loud voice, and the whole earth shook.
The Philistines heard their shouting and said, “What is this noise in the camp of the Hebrews?” And they learned that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp.
The Philistines were very afraid. They said, “These are the gods who have come to them in their camp! Woe to us! Our lord, save us today, for no such shouting occurred yesterday or the day before.
Woe to us! Who will save us from the hands of these mighty gods? These are the gods who devastated Egypt with every plague, and throughout the wilderness.
Take courage and be strong, Philistines, so that you do not become slaves to the Hebrews as they became slaves to us. Be strong men and fight them!”
And they stood firm and fought them. The men of Israel were defeated, and each went to his own tent. A very great slaughter took place among them, and thirty thousand men of Israel fell.
And the ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were killed.
A Benjaminite fled from the battle and came to Shiloh that day, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head.

Eli was sitting on his chair beside the gate, watching the road, because his heart was anxious about the ark of the Lord. The man entered the city to tell them the news, and when the city heard it, it cried out.
Eli heard the sound of the outcry and said, “What is this noise and this shouting?” The man ran and came to tell Eli.
Eli was ninety years old. His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see. Eli said to the people standing before him, “What is the sound of this shouting?”
The man ran and hurried to Eli. He said to him, “I am the man who came from the camp. I fled from the battle today.” Eli said to him, “What happened, my son?”
The young man answered him, “The men of Israel fled before the Philistines, and there was a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons have been killed, and the ark of the Lord has been taken.”
When he mentioned the ark of the Lord, Eli fell backward from his chair beside the gate. His neck broke, and he died, because he was old and heavy. He had judged Israel for twenty years.

His daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Phinehas, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news that the ark of God had been taken and that her father-in-law and her husband had died, she opened her mouth and wept. She gave birth, because severe labor pains came upon her.

She was about to die, at the end of her life. The women beside her said to her, “Do not be afraid, because you are giving birth to a son.” But she did not answer them, nor did her heart regain awareness.
The women named the little boy “Woe, Ichabod,” explaining that this was because of the ark of God, her father-in-law, and her husband.
They said, “The glory of Israel has been taken away because the ark of the Lord was captured.”
The Philistines took the ark of the Lord from Ebenezer and brought it into Ashdod.
The Philistines took the ark of the Lord, brought it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside Dagon.

The people of Ashdod rose early and hurried into the temple of Dagon. They looked, and there was Dagon lying face down before the ark of God. They raised Dagon and set him back in his place. The hand of the Lord fell heavily upon the people of Ashdod, tormenting them and afflicting their buttocks, in Ashdod and its surrounding territory.

When they rose early again in the morning, there was Dagon lying face down before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. Dagon’s head and the two palms of his hands lay detached, each separately, in front of the threshold. Both his elbows lay on top of the threshold. But the bone of Dagon’s neck had not fallen.
For this reason, the priests of Dagon and everyone who enters Dagon’s temple in Ashdod do not step on the threshold to this day. Instead, they spread their legs wide and step over the threshold.
The hand of the Lord fell heavily upon Ashdod. He afflicted them and destroyed their ships. Their countryside, or their fields, brought forth mice, and a great deadly affliction arose in their city.
When the people of Ashdod saw what had happened, they said to one another, “The ark of the God of Israel cannot remain with us, because his hand is harsh upon us and upon Dagon our god.”

They sent for the rulers of the Philistines and gathered them together. They said to them, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” The people of Gath said to them, “Let the ark of God be moved and come to us.” So the ark of God was moved to Gath.

After it had been moved, the hand of the Lord came upon them, and there was very great panic in the city. He struck the people of the city, from the least to the greatest, and afflicted them in their buttocks. The people of Gath made [?] for themselves to sit on.
They sent the ark of God to Ashkelon. The people of Ashkelon cried out, saying, “Why have you sent us the ark of the God of Israel—to kill us and the rest of our people?”

They sent for and gathered all the rulers of the Philistines and said to them, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. Let it return to its own place so that it does not kill us and the rest of our people.” For a great and very severe affliction had come upon the whole city when the ark of the God of Israel was there.
Those who were still alive and had not died developed swellings in their urinary organs, and the city's cry of suffering rose to heaven.
The ark was in the land of the Philistines for seven months, and their land produced mice.
The Philistines summoned their priests, their diviners, and their soothsayers, saying, “What shall we do with the ark of the Lord? Tell us how we should send it back to its place.”

They told them, “If you send away the ark of the Lord, the God of Israel, do not send it away empty. You must give it the prescribed offering for the affliction. Then you will have relief, and the Lord will forgive you. Otherwise, the hand of the Lord will not withdraw from you.”

They asked them, “What is the prescribed offering for the affliction that we should give it?” The diviners told them, “Give it five golden buttocks, corresponding to the number of the Philistine rulers, because sin has arisen among you, your rulers, and the rest of the people.
Also make golden mice in the likeness of the mice that are destroying your land. Give glory to the Lord, so that he may lift his hand from you, from your god, and from your land.
Why have you hardened your hearts, as Pharaoh and the Egyptians hardened their hearts? When he afflicted them, did they not release the children of Israel, and they went away?

Now take what you need and make a new cart, and take two cows that have calved, without their calves. Harness the cows to the cart, but separate their calves from them and take them back to their stalls.

Take the ark and load it onto the cart. Put the golden objects that you will give it as compensation for the affliction to one side, in a box on the cart. Send it away, driving it along, and follow it.

Watch its route. If it goes along its own road, toward Beth-shemesh, then he is the one who brought this great calamity upon us. But if it does not go that way, we will know that it was not his hand that came upon us; rather, it was a chance event that befell us.”
The Philistines did this. They took the two cows that had calved and harnessed them to the cart, but sent their calves back to their stalls.
They themselves put the ark on the cart, and they put the offering they had vowed—the golden buttocks and the golden mice—in its box.

The cows went along the road, heading toward Beth-shemesh. They remained silent as they followed a single route, and they did not turn their faces to the right or to the left. The Philistine rulers walked behind it as far as the boundaries of Beth-shemesh.
The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. They looked up and saw the ark of the Lord. They rejoiced, got up, and came out to meet it.

The cart entered the field of Hoshea, who was in Beth-shemesh, and the cows stopped there. They set a large stone beside it. They split the wood of the cart and piled it up, and offered the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord.

The Levites took the ark of the Lord, the vowed offering that was with it, and the golden objects on it, and placed them on the large stone. That day the people of Beth-shemesh brought burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord.
The five Philistine rulers watched them, and returned to Ashkelon that day.

These are the handcrafted golden tumors that the Philistines gave as an offering to the Lord because of their suffering: one tumor for Ashdod, another for Gaza, another for Gath, another for Ashkelon, and another for Ekron.

And there were golden mice corresponding to the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers, from the large fortified cities to the villages of the Perizzites, and as far as the great stone on which they placed the ark of the Lord’s covenant. It is in Joshua’s field, outside Beth-shemesh.

But the sons of Jeconiah did not rejoice with the people of Beth-shemesh because they had seen the ark of the Lord. And he struck down seventy men among them, and fifty thousand men. The people mourned because the Lord had brought a very great calamity upon the people.
The people of Beth-shemesh said to one another, “Who can walk before this holy Lord? And to whom will the ark of the Lord go up, so that it leaves us in peace?”
They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying to them, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord’s covenant to us. Come and take it up to yourselves.”

The people of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the Lord’s covenant. They brought it into Abinadab’s house on the hill, and he consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the Lord’s covenant.
From the day the ark came to be in Kiriath-jearim, many days passed, amounting to twenty years. And the whole house of Israel turned back and followed the Lord.

Samuel said to the whole house of Israel, “If you are going to return to the Lord with your whole heart, remove your foreign gods and the other sacred groves from among you. Direct your hearts toward the Lord and serve him alone, and he will rescue you from the hands of the Philistines.”
The Israelites removed the Baals and the groves of Ashtoreth and served the Lord alone.
Samuel said to them, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the Lord for you.”
They all gathered at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it onto the ground before the Lord. They fasted that day, saying, “We have sinned before the Lord.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
The Philistines heard that all the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, and the Philistine rulers came up against Israel. When the Israelites heard, they were very afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, “Do not remain silent on our behalf or stop crying out to the Lord your God, so that you may save us from the hands of the Philistines.”
Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it as a burnt offering, together with all the people, before the Lord. Samuel cried out to the Lord on behalf of Israel, and the Lord heard him.

While Samuel was offering his burnt offering, the Philistines came up against Israel to fight them. But that day the Lord thundered with a mighty sound against the Philistines. They were thrown into confusion and defeated before Israel.
The Israelites went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down until they reached Beth-car.
Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and the place called “the Old One.” He named it Ebenezer, which means “the stone of the helper,” saying, “Up to this point the Lord has helped us.”
The Lord humbled the Philistines, and they no longer continued to enter Israel’s territory. The Lord’s hand was against the Philistines throughout all the days of Samuel.

And the cities that the Philistines had taken from the Israelites, from Ashkelon as far as Azob, [?]. And they took Israel’s territory from the hands of the Philistines. There was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
He traveled around to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all the holy places.
His resting place was Ramathaim, because his house was there. He judged Israel there, and there he built an altar to the Lord.
When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
These were the names of his sons: the firstborn was Joel, and the second was Abijah. They served as judges in Beersheba.
But his sons did not follow his ways. Instead, they turned away from the truth, accepted bribes, and failed to administer justice fairly.
The Israelites gathered together and came up to Samuel at Ramathaim.
They said to him, “Look, you have grown old, and your sons have not followed your ways. Now get up and appoint a king over us to judge us, like the other nations.”
Samuel was displeased by their words when they said, “Give us a king over us to judge us.” Samuel prayed to the Lord.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to the people's voice in what they say to you, for it is not you [?] rejected, so as not to reign over them.
“Just as in everything they have done to me from the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt until today, abandoning me and serving other gods, so they are treating you too.”
Now listen to their voice, but solemnly warn them and tell them the rights of the king who will reign over them.”
Samuel told all the Lord's words to the people who were asking him for a king over them.
He said, “These are the rights of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons from you and assign them to his chariots and his horsemen, and they will run ahead of his chariots.

He will also equip them and make them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds for himself. They will plow his fields, reap his harvest, and make his weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots.
He will also take your daughters to make perfumes, cook, and bake.
He will take your fertile fields, your vineyards, and your good olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your crops and your vineyards and give it to his servants and his eunuchs.
“He will take your male servants and your female servants, your good cattle and your sheep, and put them to work for him.”
He will take a tenth of your flocks of sheep, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you chose for yourselves. But the Lord will not listen to you on that day, because you chose a king for yourselves.”
The people refused to listen to Samuel. They said to him, “We will not settle for this! Instead, there must be a king over us,
so that we too may be like all the other nations. Our king will judge us, go out ahead of us, and fight the war that rises against us.”
Samuel heard all the people's words and repeated them in the Lord's hearing.
The Lord said to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and anoint a king over them.” Samuel said to all the men of Israel, “Let each of you go back to his own town.”
There was a man from the tribe of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Sared, son of Bachir, son of Aphek, son of a Benjaminite. He was a powerful man.

He had a son named Saul, a tall man of good stature. No one among the Israelites was better-looking than he was. He stood more than a neck's height above them all, taller than anyone in the whole land.
The donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, went missing. Kish, Saul's father, said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants with you, get up, and go look for the donkeys.”

And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim. They also passed through the land of Selcha, but they did not find them. They also passed through the land of Esakem, but they did not find them. They also passed through the land of Jakim, but they did not find them.
When they came to the land of Ziph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, “Come, let us turn back and go home, or my father may stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us.”

But the servant said to him, “Look, there is a man of God in this town. That man understands everything, and everything he says comes true. Now let us go to him so that he can tell us which way we should go.”
Saul said to his servant who was with him, “Look, if we go, what will we give the man of God? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have nothing else with us to bring to the man of God.”
The servant answered Saul again, “Look, I have found a quarter of a silver stater in my hand. Take it and give it to the man of God, and he will tell us which way to go.”
Formerly in Israel, when people were going to inquire of God, each would say to his neighbor, “Come, let us go to the seer,” because formerly the people called the prophet “the seer.”
Saul said to his servant, “What you have said is good. Come, let us go.” And they went up to the town, to the house where the man of God was.
As they were walking up toward the town, they met some young girls coming out to draw water. They said to them, “Is the seer here?”
The young girls answered, “Yes, he is here. Look, he is ahead of you now. He came up to the town just today, because the people have a sacrifice today at Bamah.

“When you enter the town, you will find him there before he goes up to Bamah to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he is the one who will bless the sacrifice. After that, the guests will eat. So go up now, because you will find him today.”
And they went up to the town. When they entered the town gate, Samuel came out toward them, about to go up to Bamah.
The Lord had revealed this to Samuel a day before Saul came to him, saying to him:

“About this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Rise and anoint him as ruler over the people of Israel. He will save the people from the Philistines, because I have seen my people's humiliation, and their cry has reached me.”
Samuel saw Saul, and the Lord spoke to him, saying, “Here is the man I told you about. He is the one who will rule over my people.”
Saul approached Samuel in the middle of the town and said to him, “Tell me, which is the seer's house?”
Samuel answered Saul, “I am he. Go up ahead of me to Bamah and eat with me today. In the morning I will send you on your way and tell you everything that is in your heart.

“As for your donkeys that went missing—today is the third day—do not worry about them, because they have been found. And to whom will the honors of Israel be given? Will they not be given to you and your father's household?”
Saul answered Samuel, “Am I not the son of a Benjaminite, from the smallest division, the tribe of Benjamin, the least of all the divisions of Israel? Why have you spoken to me in these terms?”
Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the lodging place. He gave them a place of honor among the leading men who had been invited, about seventy people.
Samuel said to the cook, “Give me the portion I spoke to you about when I said, ‘Keep it with you.’”

The cook lifted up the leg, that is, the thigh, and placed it before Saul. Samuel said to Saul, “Here is what was left over, or the portion meant for you. Set it before you and eat, because it was set aside for you as a testimony, apart from the others. Take your share and eat.” And Saul ate with Samuel that day.
He came down from the high place into the town. They spread many garments for Saul on the roof.

He lay down to sleep. When daylight spread, Samuel called to Saul on the roof, saying to him, “Get up and come, so that I can send you on your way.” Saul got up and came down, and he and Samuel walked out together.
When they came to the outskirts of the town, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell your servant to walk ahead of us. But you stand here now and listen to the word of God.”

Samuel took the flask, or container, of oil and poured it over Saul’s head. He kissed him and said to him, “The Lord has anointed you to rule over his people Israel. You will lead the people of Israel and save them from the hands of their enemies around them. This will be the sign for you that the Lord has anointed you to rule over his inheritance:

When you leave me today, you will find two men near Rachel’s tomb in the hill country of Benjamin, leaping greatly for joy. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you went to look for have been found. Your father has stopped worrying about the animals and is very worried about you, saying, “What shall I do about my son?”’

You will go on from that place and come to the tree of Tabor. There you will meet three men going to God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another will be carrying three containers of bread, and the other will be carrying a skin of wine.
They will greet you with wishes for peace and give you two loaves of bread as a first offering. You are to accept them from their hands.

After this, you are to go into the hill of God, where the Philistines’ outpost is, with Nasib the Philistine in that place. When you enter the town from there, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place. Ahead of them will be lyres, drums, reed flutes, and a harp, and they will be prophesying.
The Spirit of the Lord will come down upon you, and you will prophesy with them. You will be changed and become a different person.
When these signs happen to you, do whatever good things your hand finds to do, because God will be with you.

You are to go ahead of me down to Gilgal. Look, I will come to you there to offer a burnt offering and sacrifices of peace offerings. You must wait seven days until I come to you, and I will tell you what you are to do.”
When Saul turned his head to go away from him, God gave him a different heart, and all these signs happened to him that day.
He went from that place to the hill, and there was a group of prophets ahead of him. The Spirit of God rushed down upon him, and he prophesied among them.

Everyone who had known him before saw him, and there he was among the prophets. The people said to one another, “What is this that has happened to the son of Kish? Has Saul too been counted among the prophets?”
One of them answered, “And who is his father?” Because of this, the saying became a proverb: “Has Saul been counted among the prophets?”
When he finished prophesying, he went up to the hill.
Kish, his father, said to him and to the other man with him, “Where did you go?” He said to him, “We went to look for the donkeys. When we saw that we could not find them, we went to Samuel.”
Kish said to Saul, “Tell me what Samuel said to you.”
Saul said to his father, “He told me plainly that the donkeys had been found.” But he did not reveal to him what had been said about the kingship.
And Samuel instructed all the people to come before the Lord at Mizpah.

Samuel said to the Israelites, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought the Israelites out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the power of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and from the power of all the kingdoms that oppress you.’

“But today you have rejected God, who saves you from all your hardships and troubles, and you have said, ‘We will not remain as we are; instead, appoint a king over us.’ Now stand before the Lord according to your tribes and the thousands of your clans.”
Samuel brought forward the whole congregation of Israel, and the lot fell on the congregation of Benjamin.

He brought forward the congregation of Benjamin according to its clans, and the lot fell on the clan of Matri. He brought forward the clan of Matri, man by man, and the lot fell on Saul, the son of Kish. They looked for him but did not find him.
Samuel turned back and asked the Lord, “Will the man come here?” The Lord said to him, “Look, he is hiding among the baggage.”
Samuel ran and brought him out of that place and stood him among the people. He was taller than all the people by a neck’s length.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the man the Lord has chosen for himself? There is no one like him among all of you.” All the people understood and shouted, “Long live the king!”
Samuel explained to all the people the regulations of kingship. He wrote them in a book and placed it before the Lord. Then Samuel dismissed all the people, and each went home.
Saul also went to his home in Gibeah. Strong men, into whose hearts God had put this, went and followed Saul.
But some worthless men spoke up, saying, “Who will save us? This man?” They insulted him and brought him no gifts.
After a month, Nahash the Ammonite came up and advanced against Jabesh in Gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash the Ammonite, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
Nahash the Ammonite said to them, “I will make the treaty with you on condition that each of you gouges out his right eye, so that I may bring disgrace on Israel.”
The men of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days, and we will send messengers throughout all the territories of Israel. If they do not rescue us, we will come out to you.”
The messengers from Jabesh came to Saul at Gibeah and reported these words in the hearing of the people. All the people raised their voices and wept.
Saul came in from the field after the morning hour. Saul said, “Why are the people weeping?” They told him everything the people of Jabesh had said.
The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned fiercely.

He took two cattle and cut them into pieces. They sent the pieces throughout all the territories of Israel by the messengers, while he said, “Whoever does not come out to follow Saul and Samuel will have the same thing done to his cattle.” The fear of the Lord fell upon the people of Israel, and they all cried out together as one man.
Abiezek counted them in Bama. All the men of Israel numbered six hundred thousand, and the men of Judah numbered seventy thousand.

He said to the messengers who had come, “This is what you are to tell the men of Jabesh: ‘Tomorrow you will be rescued when the sun gives its heat.’” The messengers went to their city and reported these words to the men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.
The men of Jabesh said to Nahash the Ammonite, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and we will do whatever pleases you.”

The next day, Saul divided the people into three companies and entered the camp early in the morning. They struck down the Ammonites until the sun grew hot. Those who survived were scattered, and no two of them remained together.
The people said to Samuel, “Who said, ‘Saul will not reign over us’? Hand those men over to us so that we can kill them.”
Saul said, “No one will die today, because today the Lord has brought salvation to Israel.”
Samuel said to the people, “Let us go up to Gilgal, and I will establish the kingship there.”

All the people went up to Gilgal, and there Samuel anointed Saul to be king before the Lord at Gilgal. He slaughtered sacrifices of peace offerings there before the Lord, and Samuel and all Israel rejoiced greatly.
Samuel said to all the people of Israel, “Look, I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me, and I have appointed a king over you.”
Now, here is your king; he will lead you. But I have grown old, and I will sit down and rest. My sons are here among you. As for me, I have been among you from my youth until this very day.

Here I am today, standing before you. Speak against me before the Lord and before his anointed one. Have I taken anyone’s ox or anyone’s donkey? Have I taken anything from any of you by force? Have I oppressed anyone? Have I taken a bribe from anyone, or taken anyone’s sandal? If so, say it, and I will return it to you.
They all said to Samuel, “You have not treated us unjustly in any way, nor have you caused us any hardship. You have not oppressed anyone or taken anything belonging to anyone.”
Samuel said to the people, “The Lord is a witness among you today, and his anointed one is a witness, that today you have found no act of injustice in my hands.” They all said, “He is a witness.”
Samuel said to the people, “The Lord God is the one who made Moses and Aaron, the one who brought our ancestors out of Egypt.
Now stand still, and I will present my case against you before the Lord. I will recount to you all the Lord’s righteous deeds, the things he did for you and your ancestors.

When Jacob and his sons went into Egypt, and Egypt oppressed them, our ancestors cried out to the Lord. The Lord sent Moses and Aaron, and they brought our ancestors out of Egypt, and the Lord settled them in this place.

But they forgot the Lord their God, and the Lord handed them over to Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin, king of Hazor, and to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, who fought against them.
They cried out to the Lord, saying, ‘We have sinned, because we have abandoned the Lord and served the Baals and the groves. Now rescue us from the hands of our enemies, and we will serve you.’
Then the Lord sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel. He rescued you from the hands of your enemies around you, and you lived securely.
But when you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had come against you, you said, ‘We will not remain like this; instead, a king will reign over us,’ even though the Lord our God was our king.
Now here is the king you chose for yourselves. Look, the Lord has set a king over you.
Fear the Lord, serve him, obey his voice, and do not rebel against the Lord’s command. Both you and your king who will reign over you must continue to follow the Lord.
But if you do not obey the Lord’s voice and rebel against the Lord’s command, the Lord’s hand will be against you and against your king.
Now stand still and see this great thing that the Lord will do before your eyes.

Is today not the wheat harvest? Look, I will call on the Lord, and he will send thunder and rain, so that you may understand and see how great the evil you have done is before the Lord, by asking for a king over you.
Samuel called on the Lord, and the Lord sent thunder and rain that day. All the people were greatly afraid of the Lord and of Samuel.
All the people said to Samuel, “Pray to the Lord your God for your servants, so that we do not die. For we have added to all our sins and our wickedness by asking for a king over us.”
Samuel said to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil, but do not turn aside and withdraw from the Lord. Instead, serve the Lord with all your heart.”
Do not go after things that do not exist. They cannot do anything and cannot save you, for they are not gods.
“For the Lord will not abandon his people, because of his great name. For, as the Lord has done, he has taken you to himself as his people because of his great name.”
As for me, may I never sin against the Lord by stopping praying for you. Instead, I will serve the Lord and teach you the good and straight way.
Only fear the Lord and serve him faithfully and with all your heart, for you have seen the wonderful things he has done among you.
“But if you and your kings sin wickedly, the Lord will bring your enemies against you.”

Saul chose three thousand men for himself from the men of Israel. Two thousand men followed Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand men were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people away, each to his own home.

Jonathan struck Nasib the Philistine, who lived on the hill, and the Philistines heard about it. Saul sounded a trumpet throughout the whole land, saying, “The slaves have rebelled and raised their heads!”
All Israel heard that Saul had struck Nasib the Philistine and destroyed him, and that they had put the Philistines to shame. The people cried out to rally behind Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered for war to fight against Israel. They rose and went against Israel with thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen, and their troops were as numerous as the sand of the sea. They came and camped at Michmash, opposite Beth-aven, to its south.
The men of Israel saw that they could not stand against them. The people of Israel hid in caves, holes, pits, and wells.
Those who were fleeing crossed the Jordan and went into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people following him were trembling.
The seven days specified in the declaration came to an end, just as Samuel had told him.
Saul said, “Bring them, so that I may offer the burnt offerings and the peace offerings.” And Saul offered the burnt offering.
When he had finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to meet him and greet him.

Samuel said to him, “What have you done?” Saul said, “Because I saw that the people had gone away and left me, and you had not come to me within the appointed days, as you had declared to me, and the Philistines had gathered at Michmash,
I said, ‘Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the Lord’s favor.’ So I forced myself to offer the burnt offerings.”

Samuel said to Saul, “You have gained nothing, because you have not kept my command, which the Lord commanded you to follow. Now the Lord had prepared your kingship to remain yours over Israel forever.

But now your kingship will not endure. The Lord will seek for himself a man after his own heart, and the Lord will appoint him to rule over his people, because you have not kept the commands that the Lord commanded you to follow.”

Samuel rose and went on his way from Gilgal. The rest of the people went up, following Saul to meet their fighting men. They went from Gilgal up to Gibeah in the land of Benjamin. Saul counted the people who were found with him, about six hundred men.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the people who were found with them stayed at Gibeah in the land of Benjamin and wept. The Philistines camped at Michmash.
The raiders came out from the Philistine countryside in three bands. One band headed toward the road to Ophrah, in the land of Shual.
Another band headed toward the road to Beth-horon, and the other band headed toward the road to Gibeah, which slopes down into the valley of Samin.
No blacksmith could be found anywhere in the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not make swords or spears.”
All Israel would go down to the land of the Philistines, each person to sharpen his sickle, and each person to sharpen his axe, his adze, and his working tool.
The harvest, or the reaping, had arrived, ready to be reaped. For their implements, a tooth cost three staters of [?], and the axe and the sickle had the same rate.

During the days of the battle at Michmash, no sword or spear could be found in the hands of any of the people who went with Saul and his son Jonathan. But they were found in the possession of Saul and his son Jonathan.
Jonathan came out from among the Philistines at the edge of Michmash. He did not tell his father.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, said to his servant who carried his armor, “Come with me, and let us go up to the Philistine outpost on the other side.”
Saul was sitting at the edge of the hill, beneath the pomegranate tree in Magdon, and six hundred men were with him.
Ahijah, the son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, God’s priest in Shiloh, was carrying the ephod. The people did not know

that Jonathan was going. In the middle of the road, at the place where Jonathan wanted to go up to the Philistine force, there was a rocky crag on either side. One was named Bozez, and the other was named Seneh.
One of the roads led northward up to Michmash, and the other led from the south up to Gibeah.

Jonathan said to his servant who carried his armor, “Come, let us go up to the outpost, the place of these uncircumcised men, and [?] what the Lord will do for us. For nothing prevents the Lord from saving those in distress through many or through few.”
His armor-bearer said to him, “Do everything your heart wants to do. Look, I am following you, and my heart is joined to your heart.”
Jonathan said to him, “Look, we will go to the men and approach them.
If they say to us, ‘Stand over there until we speak to you,’ we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say to us, ‘Come up to us,’ we will go up to them, because the Lord has handed them over to us. This will be our sign.”
The two of them went up to the outpost, the place of the Philistines. The Philistines said to one another, “Look, the Hebrews have come up from the holes where they were hiding.”

The men at the outpost, which was their guard station, said to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us, and we will teach you something.” Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, “Follow me, because the Lord has handed them over to Israel.”

Jonathan climbed up to them, keeping his hands and feet firmly planted, and his armor-bearer followed him. The Philistines stumbled before Jonathan. Jonathan struck them down, and his armor-bearer helped him.
In the first attack, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men with missiles, thrown stones, and pebbles from the field.

Terror arose in the camp and in the countryside. All the people at the outpost, along with the fighting men, were also thrown into confusion. They did not want to suffer hardship. The earth trembled, and terror from the Lord came upon them.
Saul’s watchmen in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and saw the camp in confusion, moving this way and that.
Saul said to the people who were with him, “Check your numbers and see who among you has gone.” They checked, and found that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ephod here,” for he was carrying the ephod before Israel that day.
While Saul was speaking with the priest, a very loud noise arose in the Philistine camp. Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.”
Saul went up with all the people who were with him, and they reached the battlefield. There, each man's sword was turned against his fellow, and great confusion arose among them.

The other slaves who had been with the Philistines yesterday and three days before, who had gone up with them into the camp, also changed sides and joined the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.
All the Israelites who were hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines had fled, and they too ran after them into battle.

The Lord saved Israel that day, and the battle reached as far as Beth-on. The entire crowd marching with Saul numbered about ten thousand men, and the battle spread throughout the whole city in the hill country of Ephraim.

Saul acted with great ignorance that day. He put the people under an oath, saying, “Cursed is anyone who eats bread before evening, so that I may take revenge on my enemy.” None of the people tasted bread.
The whole land was eating its meal, and there was a wooded place producing honey in front of the field.
The people went up to the place where honey was produced. They walked along talking, but no one brought his hand to his mouth, because the people were afraid of the oath sworn by the Lord.

Jonathan had not heard that his father had put the people under oath. Jonathan stretched out the tip of the staff in his hand and dipped it into the honeycomb. He brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes could see and became bright.
One of the people said to him, “Your father solemnly put the people under oath, saying, ‘Cursed is anyone who eats bread today.’” The people had grown weak.
Jonathan understood and said, “My father has brought trouble on the land. Look how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
If the people had eaten freely today from the plunder they found belonging to their enemies, the slaughter of the Philistines would now have been greater.”
He struck down some of the Philistines that day at Michmash, and the people became very exhausted.
The people rushed upon the plunder. They took flocks of sheep, cattle, and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. The people ate the meat with its blood.
They informed Saul, saying to him, “The people have sinned against the Lord by eating the meat with its blood.” Saul said to them, “Bring a large stone here from Gathaim.”

Saul said to them, “Go out among the people and tell them, ‘Let each of you bring his ox and his sheep to his place and slaughter it on this stone, so that you do not sin against the Lord by eating it with its blood.’” Each of the people brought what he had, and they slaughtered them at that place.
Saul built an altar to the Lord at that place. This was the first altar Saul began to build to the Lord.

Saul said to the people, “Let us attack the Philistines tonight and plunder them until morning, and let us not leave a single one of them alive.” They said to him, “Do whatever seems good to you.” The priest said, “Let us approach God here and ask him.”
Saul asked God, “Should I go against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into Israel's hands?” But the Lord did not answer him that day.
Saul said to them, “Bring all the divisions of Israel here, and find out and see who committed this sin today.
For as the Lord lives, who saved Israel, even if he tells us that it concerns Jonathan my son, he will surely die.” Not one person among all the people spoke.
Saul said to all the men of Israel, “You will be in slavery, and I too, along with Jonathan my son, will be in slavery.” The people said to Saul, “Do what seems good to you.”

Saul said, “Lord, God of Israel, why have you not spoken with your servant today? If the sin rests on me or on Jonathan my son, Lord, God of Israel, give us a sign. And if you say concerning these people, ‘This is how it will be,’ give a sign, Lord, to your people Israel.” The lot fell on Jonathan and Saul, and the people were cleared.

Saul said, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son. Whoever the Lord causes the lot to fall on must die.” The people said to Saul, “This must not happen!” But Saul compelled the people, and they cast lots between him and Jonathan his son. The lot fell on Jonathan.
Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan told him, saying, “I dipped the tip of my staff into a little honey and tasted it. And now, look, I am going to die because of this.”
Saul said to him, “May God do this to me and add still more to it, for you will certainly die today.”

The people said to Saul, “Will the man who brought about this great deliverance in Israel die today [?]? As the Lord lives, not a single hair from his head will fall to the ground, for God's people have committed this great sin.” The people prayed to God on Jonathan's behalf that day, and he did not die.
Saul went to the Philistines, and the Philistines went up to their own places.

Saul was chosen by lot to reign, and he became a great figure over Israel. He fought against all his enemies around him: Moab, the Ammonites, the Edomites, Beth-hor, the king of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he went, he was victorious.
He performed a mighty feat, struck down Amalek, and rescued Israel from the hands of those who oppressed them.
These were Saul's sons: Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. These were the names of his two daughters: the firstborn was named Merab, and the second was named Michal.
His wife's name was Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of his army commander was Abner, the son of Ner, the son of Saul's female servant.
Kish was Saul's father, and Ner was Abner's father, the son of Jabin, the son of Abiel.
The war against the Philistines was fierce throughout Saul's days. Whenever Saul saw any capable man or any strong man, he gathered them together.
Samuel said to Saul, “The Lord sent me to anoint you king over Israel. Now, therefore, listen to the voice of the Lord.
“This is what the Lord of hosts said: ‘Now I will repay Amalek for what he did to Israel, for the way he confronted Israel on the road as Israel was coming out of Egypt.

“‘Now, therefore, go and strike down Amalek and Jerim and everything that belongs to him. Do not spare any of them. Wipe him out, and utterly condemn him to destruction along with everything that belongs to him. Do not show him mercy. Kill men and women, young children and nursing infants, cattle and sheep, camels and donkeys.’”
Saul summoned his people and mustered them at Gibeah. Israel numbered four hundred thousand people, and Judah numbered thirty thousand people.
Saul came to the cities of Amalek and set an ambush in the ravine.

Saul said to the Kenites, “Get up and come out from among Amalek, so that I do not destroy you along with him. You showed kindness to the Israelites when they came out of Egypt.” So the Kenites got up and came out from among Amalek.
Saul struck down Amalek from Havilah as far as Shur, which is opposite Egypt.
And he captured Agag, the king of Amalek, alive, and killed all his people with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and all his people spared Agag alive, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, their food supplies, their vineyards, and all their good things. He was unwilling to destroy them. But everything that was not choice and was worthless, he destroyed.
And the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying to him:
“I regret that I anointed Saul to become king, because he has turned away and withdrawn from me and has not kept my words.” Samuel was distressed, and he cried out to the Lord all night.

And Samuel rose early and went to Israel in the morning. Saul was told, “Samuel has gone up to Carmel, and look, Saul has prepared to purify himself. He has turned his chariot around and come down to Gilgal.”

And Samuel came to Saul. Saul was offering his rich burnt offering to the Lord from the choicest spoils that he had brought up from Amalek. And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, “You are blessed by the Lord. I have fulfilled the word that the Lord spoke.”
Samuel said to him, “What is this sound of the flock of sheep reaching my ears, and the sound of these cattle that I hear?”
Saul said to him, “I brought them from Amalek. The people spared the best of the flocks of sheep and cattle to offer them as sacrifices to the Lord your God. But I destroyed all the rest.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Wait, and I will tell you the words that the Lord spoke to me during the night.” He said to him, “Tell me.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Were you not small before the multitude of the tribe of Israel? Yet the Lord anointed you to become king over Israel.
And the Lord sent you on his way, saying to you, ‘Go and destroy and wipe out those who sin against me, namely Amalek. Fight against them until you have finished them off.’
Why, then, did you not obey the voice of the Lord, but rush upon the spoils to take them and do evil in the Lord’s sight?”
Saul said to Samuel, “Because I obeyed the voice of the people and walked along the way on which the Lord sent me. I brought Agag [?], the king of Amalek, alive, and I wiped out Amalek.
But the people took from the spoils flocks of sheep and cattle, the choicest plunder, to offer them as a sacrifice to the Lord our God in Gilgal.”
Samuel said to him, “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings as much as obedience to the Lord’s voice? Obedience is better than a good sacrifice, and paying attention is better than the fat of rams.
For sin is divination, and distress and toil bring about hardship. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord will also reject you, so that you will not be king over Israel.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, because I disregarded the word of the Lord and put your word behind me, because I was afraid of the people and obeyed their voice.
Now, then, forgive my sin and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord your God.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord. The Lord will also reject you, so that you will not be king over Israel.”
And Samuel turned away from him to leave, but Saul grabbed the edge of his robe and tore it.
Samuel said to him, “Today the Lord has torn your kingship over Israel from your hand and given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.
And Israel will be divided in two. The Lord will not turn back, nor will he show mercy, because he is not like a human being who regrets his decision when he becomes angry.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned, Lord. But honor me now before the elders of Israel and before the people, and return with me, so that I may worship the Lord your God.”
And Samuel returned with Saul, and he worshiped the Lord.
Samuel said to them, “Bring me Agag, the king of Amalek.” Agag approached him trembling, and Agag said to him, “So death is bitter like this?”
Samuel said to him, “Because your sword has made many women childless, your mother will likewise be childless among women.” And Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the Lord at Gilgal.
Afterward Samuel went to Ramathaim, while Saul went up to his house in Gibeah.
Samuel did not return to see Saul again until the day of his death. Samuel mourned over Saul, and the Lord regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.

The Lord said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn over Saul, when I have rejected him as king? Now fill your horn with oil and come, so that I may send you to Jesse in Bethlehem. For among Jesse’s sons I have chosen one who will be king for me.”
Samuel said to the Lord, “How can I go? Saul will hear and kill me.” The Lord said to him, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord.’
“Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will tell you what you are to do. Anoint the one I indicate to you.”
Samuel did everything the Lord had told him and went up to Bethlehem. The elders of the city were astonished when they saw him, and they said to him, “Is your coming peaceful, seer?”
He said to them, “Peace! I have come to offer a sacrifice to the Lord. Purify yourselves and rejoice with me today.” He purified Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they came in, he saw Eliab and said about him, “Surely here is the Lord’s anointed before him.”

The Lord said to Samuel, “Do not look at his appearance or his great height, because he is rejected in my sight. God does not look as people do, looking at the face. People look only at the face, but God looks at the heart.”
Jesse called Amminadab, and he came and stood before Samuel. Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had Shammah stand there. Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had his seven sons stand before Samuel. Samuel said, “The Lord has not chosen any of these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are these all your sons?” Jesse said to him, “There is still the youngest of them, and he is tending the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send for him, because we will not sit down to eat until he comes.”
He sent for him and brought him up. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and pleasing to look at in the Lord’s sight. The Lord said to Samuel, “Get up and anoint David, for he is a good man.”
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David among his brothers. The Spirit of the Lord came powerfully upon David from that day onward. Samuel went up to Ramathaim.
The Spirit of the Lord withdrew from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord tormented him.
Saul’s servants said to him, “Look, an evil spirit from the Lord is tormenting you.

“Let your servants speak before you and look for a man who knows how to play a lyre, so that we may bring him before our lord. When the evil spirit comes upon you, he will play his lyre and give you relief.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who knows how to play well, and bring him to me.”

One of his servants answered him, “Look, I have seen a son of Jesse from Bethlehem who knows how to play. He is an intelligent man and a warrior, wise in his speech and handsome in appearance, and the Lord is with him.”
Saul sent messengers to Jesse, saying, “Send me your son David, who is with your sheep.”
Jesse took a measure of bread, a wineskin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to Saul through his son David.
David went in to Saul and stood before him. Saul loved him very much, and David served under him, carrying his weapons.
Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David stay with me, because he has found favor with me.”
Whenever the evil spirit came upon Saul, David would take his lyre in his hand and play it. Saul would find relief and feel better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered in their camps, or their battle lines, for war. They came up to Socoh in Idumea, between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered in the valley of the mountain and took their positions for battle opposite the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one side of the mountain, and Israel stood on the other side of the mountain. The ravine, that is, the valley, was between them.
A champion, a mighty man, came out from the Philistine ranks. His name was Goliath, and he was from Gath. His height was four cubits and a span.
He had a helmet on his head and wore a coat of scale armor. The weight of his armor was five thousand staters of bronze.
Bronze greaves were fastened to his legs, and an iron shield rested between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its spearhead weighed six hundred staters of iron. The man carrying his weapons walked ahead of him.

Goliath stood and shouted to the multitude of Israel, saying to them, “Why are you coming out and taking your positions for battle to fight us? Am I not a Philistine, while you are Hebrews, Saul’s servants? Choose a man from among you, then, and let him come out to me.
If he can fight me and strike me down, we will become your slaves. But if I overpower him and strike him down, you will become our slaves.”
The Philistine said to them, “Look, today I have challenged the people of Israel! Bring a man out to me, and let the two of us fight together.”
Saul and all Israel heard these words from the Philistine, and they were shaken and very afraid.
David was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who had eight sons. In Saul’s days, this man was old and advanced in years.
Jesse’s three oldest sons went and followed Saul to the war. The names of his three sons who went out to the war were Eliab, the firstborn; Abinadab, the second; and Shammah, the third.
David was the youngest of them. The three older brothers went and followed Saul.
David left Saul and went to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem.
The Philistine came forward against them every day, morning and evening, for forty days.
Jesse said to his son David, “Take this measure of roasted grain for your brothers, and these ten loaves of bread. Get up and hurry to the camp, to your brothers.
Take these ten rounds of cheese to the commander of a thousand. Bring news of your brothers’ well-being, see what they lack, and bring me news of them.”
Saul, together with them and all Israel, was in the Valley of the Tall Tree, fighting the Philistines.

David rose early in the morning and left the sheep in the care of the keepers. He took the things and went, just as Jesse had instructed him. He came up to the circular enclosure, that is, the place where things are brought in, and to the ranks of those going out to battle. They raised a battle cry.
Israel and the Philistines took their positions to fight one another.
David left his belongings with the keeper of the baggage and ran out to the camp. He reached his brothers and asked about their well-being.
While he was speaking with them, the champion came out—the Philistine named Goliath, from Gath, who belonged to the Philistine ranks. He addressed them with these same words, and Saul heard him.
and all the men of Israel. When they saw the man, they ran away from him and were very afraid.

The men of Israel said to one another, “Have you seen this man who has come up against us? He has come up against Israel. The king will make the man who goes out and strikes him down very wealthy. He will give him his daughter as his wife, and he will make his father’s entire household free in Israel.”

David said to the men standing with him, “What will be done for the man who strikes down that Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine who has insulted the army of the living God?”
The people answered him in the same terms, saying, “This is what will be done for the man who strikes down this Philistine.”

Eliab, his older brother, heard him speaking with the men. Eliab became furious with David and said to him, “Why have you come down here? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart. You have come to watch the battle.”
But David said to him, “What sin have I committed? Haven’t I only said something?”
He turned away from him and went up to another man. He asked the same question, and the people answered him as they had the first time.
The words David had spoken became known and were reported to Saul. Saul had him brought in to him.
David said before Saul, “Do not let my lord lose heart because of him. I, your servant, will go and fight this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You cannot go and fight this Philistine, because you are a young boy, while he has been a warrior since his youth.”
David said to Saul, “I, your servant, used to tend my father’s sheep. Whenever a lion or a bear came and took a sheep from among them,
I would go after it and strike the lion, so that what the lion had seized came out of its mouth. If it turned against me, I would seize it by its beard, overpower it, and kill it.

your servant struck down both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them. I will go out against him, strike him down, take his head, and remove this disgrace from Israel today. For who is this uncircumcised man who has insulted the army of the living God?”

David also said, “The Lord who rescued me from the lion’s mouth and from the bear’s grasp will also rescue me from the grasp of this uncircumcised Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go out against him, and may the Lord be with you.”
Saul dressed David in an embroidered tunic and put a bronze helmet on his head.

He also put armor on him and fastened his sword over David’s armor. David stumbled when he tried to walk in them, because he had not tried them before. After walking in them once or twice, he grew tired. David said to Saul, “I cannot walk with these things on me, because I am not used to them.” So David took them off.

He took his staff in his hands and chose five smooth stones from the stream. He put them into the bag he used when tending sheep, which he had with him. With his sling in his hand, he went out toward the Philistine.
The Philistine also advanced toward David, boasting, with his shield-bearer ahead of him.
The Philistine looked and saw David, and he despised him because he was a young boy, ruddy and handsome to look at.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I like a dog that you come out against with a club and stones?” David said to him, “Perhaps you are worse than a dog.” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to him, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth.”

But David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, a spear, and a shield, but I come against you in the name of the Lord of Hosts, the God of the army of Israel, whom you have insulted today.”

And today the Lord will hand you over to me and let me kill you and take off your head. Today I will give your remains and the remains of the Philistine camp to the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth, so that the whole earth will know that there is a God in Israel.
And this whole assembly will know that the Lord does not save people by sword or spear, for the battle belongs to the Lord, and he will hand you over to us.
The Philistine got up and advanced toward David, and David hurried forward, came into the middle of the battlefield, and advanced toward the Philistine.

David reached into his bag, took a single stone from it, put it in his sling, and hurled it at the Philistine. He struck him in the forehead, and the stone drove the helmet into his forehead. He fell face down.
David defeated the Philistine with his sling and his stone. He brought the Philistine down and killed him, though David had no sword in his hand.

He ran and stood over the Philistine, grasped his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they cried out and fled.

The men of Israel and the men of Judah rose up, shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as the road leading into Gath, advancing into it, and as far as the gates of Ashkelon. The slain Philistines fell along the road of the gates, as far as Gath and Ekron.
The men of Israel returned from pursuing the Philistines, went to their camps, and plundered them.
And David took the Philistine’s head and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put his equipment in the tent.
The dancers came out from all the cities of Israel to meet David, joyfully bringing their tambourines and cymbals.
And their women sat singing and laughing, saying, “Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.”
These words greatly displeased Saul because of what they had said. He said, “They have credited David with tens of thousands, but they have credited me with thousands.”
From that day onward, Saul’s heart was hostile toward David.
After that day, an evil spirit came upon Saul, and he prophesied in the middle of his house, again as he did every day. The spear was in Saul’s hand.
Saul looked at the spear and said, “I will strike David with this.” But when he threw it at David, David dodged away from Saul, and it struck the wall.
And Saul was afraid of David.
He removed him from his presence and appointed him commander of a thousand men. David went out and came in at the head of the people.
David acted wisely in all his ways, and the Lord was with him.
When Saul saw that David acted very wisely, he became afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David because he came in and went out at the head of the people.

Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you as your wife. Only be a brave son to me and fight against the Lord’s enemies.” But Saul said, “My hand must not be against him.”
David said, “Who am I, and what is my father’s family in Israel, that I should marry the king’s daughter?”
When the time came for Merab, Saul’s daughter, to marry David, she was given to Adriel [?], son of Maollais [?], to be his wife.
And Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David. They told Saul about this, and it pleased him.
Saul said, “I will give her to him as his wife so that she will become a trap for him.” And the hand of the Philistines was against Saul.
Saul instructed his servants, saying to them, “Speak privately with David and tell him, ‘Look, the king wants you, and all his other servants love you. So agree to marry the king’s daughter.’”
Saul’s servants spoke to David in these words. David said to them, “Do you consider it a small matter for me to become related to the king in this way? I am a poor man, despised and without honor.”
And Saul’s servants told Saul the words David had spoken.

Saul said to them, “This is what you are to say to David: ‘The king does not want this marriage arrangement to be settled with money, but with a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on the king’s enemies.’” But Saul was plotting to hand him over to the Philistines.
Saul’s servants told David these words, and David was pleased at the prospect of becoming the king’s son-in-law.

David got up and went with his men. He killed a hundred Philistine men and brought their foreskins before the king. He became the king’s son-in-law, and the king gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Saul saw that the Lord was with David and that all Israel loved him.
Saul became even more afraid of David.
Saul spoke to his son Jonathan and all his servants about killing David.
