But Jonathan, Saul’s son, loved David very much. Jonathan told David, “Saul is seeking to kill you. So be on your guard tomorrow morning. Withdraw and stay in a hiding place.
I will stand beside my father and come to you in the field, to the place where you will be. I will also speak to my father about you and see what he says, and I will report the outcome to you.”
Jonathan spoke favorably about David to his father Saul, saying to him, “Do not let the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and his deeds are very good.

You know that he took his life in his hands, went out, and struck down the Philistine, and the Lord brought about a great deliverance for Israel. They saw the deliverance and rejoiced. Why, then, would you sin against innocent blood by killing David like this for no reason?”
Saul listened to his son Jonathan, and Saul swore, saying, “As the Lord lives, David will not die.”
Jonathan called David and told him all these words. Jonathan brought David before Saul, and he was in Saul’s presence as he had been in days past.
War broke out again. David grew strong and fought against the Philistines. He struck them with a very great blow, and they fled from him.
An evil spirit came upon Saul while he was lying asleep in his house with his spear in his hand. David was playing the instrument in his hands.
Saul sought a way to strike David with the spear in his hand, but David moved aside from Saul. Saul’s spear lodged in the wall. David withdrew and escaped, and the spear was pulled out of the wall.

That night Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him so that he could kill him in the morning. But his wife Michal told David, “If you do not save your life tonight, they will kill you tomorrow.”
Michal lowered David through the window. He got up, fled, and saved himself.
Michal took the funerary images and put them on the bed. She placed a goat’s liver on top of it and covered it with a garment.
Saul sent messengers to bring David to him. They said, “He is sick.”
Saul sent messengers after David, telling them, “Lift him onto this bed and bring him to me so that I can kill him.”
The messengers came, and there were the funerary images on the bed, with a goat’s liver lying beneath his head.
Saul said to Michal, “Why have you deceived me like this and let my enemy go, so that he escaped?” Michal said to her father Saul, “He was the one who told me, ‘Let me go away, or I will kill you.’”
David fled and escaped. He came to Samuel at Ramathaim and told him everything Saul had done to him. David and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth in Ramah.
Saul was told, “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul sent messengers to capture David. They saw the assembly of prophets, with Samuel standing over them. The Spirit of God came upon Saul’s messengers, and they too prophesied.
When Saul was told what had happened, he sent other messengers, and they too prophesied. Saul went on to send other messengers a third time, and they too prophesied.
Saul rushed out in anger and went himself to Ramathaim. He came to the well of the threshing floor in Sephi. Saul asked, “Where is Samuel?” They told him, “Look, he is in Naioth in Ramah.”
Saul went up to Naioth in Ramah, and the Spirit of God came upon him too. He walked along prophesying until he reached Naioth in Ramah.
He stripped off his clothes and continued prophesying before Samuel. He fell down and lay naked all that day and all that night. That is why people said, “Is Saul too among the prophets?”
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came to Jonathan. He said to him, “What have I done? What wrong have I committed, or what is my sin against your father, that he is seeking to take my life?”

Jonathan said, “You have done nothing. You will not die. Look, my father will do nothing, great or small, without telling me about it. Why, then, would my father hide this matter from me? Surely that is not so!”

David answered Jonathan, “Your father knows that I have found favor with you, and your father has said, ‘Do not let Jonathan know about this, so that he does not tell David about it.’ But as the Lord lives and as you live, just as I have said, his evil purpose has fully developed between me and death.”
Jonathan said to David, “What do you want me to do for you?”
David said to Jonathan, “Look, tomorrow is the first day of the month, and I am not going to sit down to eat with the king. Send me away so that I can hide in the field until the time of your [?].”
If your father makes inquiries about me, tell him, “He earnestly asked me to let him go to Bethlehem, his town, because a sacrifice for the whole clan will take place there at the appointed time.”
“If he says, ‘Good, let him go,’ then your servant will be safe. But if he speaks harshly to you, know that he has fully resolved on evil.”

“Show kindness to your servant, because you have brought your servant into a covenant of the Lord with you. If your servant is guilty of wrongdoing, kill me yourself. Why should you bring me before your father like this?”
Jonathan said to him, “May that never happen to me! If I know for certain that my father has fully resolved to bring harm upon you—even if he is not in your cities—I will tell you about it.”
David said to Jonathan, “Who will tell me about this if your father speaks harshly to you?”
Jonathan said to David, “Come, let us go out into the field.” So the two of them went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, “The Lord, the God of Israel, knows that I will question or approach my father when the time comes for me, three times [?]. If something favorable is said about David, I will send [?] to you out in the field.”

“May God do these things to Jonathan, and may he add still more to me! I will tell you about the evil things and disclose them to you. I will send you away, and you will go in peace. May the Lord be with you as he was with my father.”
And while I am still alive, you will show me mercy, but also in death, if I die.
“Never withdraw your kindness from my household, even when the Lord removes David’s enemies, every one of them, from the face of the earth.”
“Let Jonathan’s name not be removed from David’s household, and may the Lord call David to account concerning his enemies.”
Jonathan again swore an oath to David because he loved him, and he loved the life of the one who loved him.
Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the first day of the month. They will ask about you because they will notice your seat.”
“When you have stayed there for three days, go down to the place where you hid on the day of the work, and stay beside Ergab there.”
“I will do it three times, shooting the arrows toward a target.”

And look, I will send my servant out, saying, “Come and find the arrows for me.” If I speak to the young boy and say, “The arrow is on this side of you, on this other side; pick it up and come,” then get up and come, because you are safe, and there is no threat against you, as the Lord lives.
But if I say these words to the servant, “The arrow is on that side of you, beyond you,” then get up and go, because the Lord has sent you away.
And concerning the agreement that you and I have made, look, the Lord is a witness between me and you forever.
David hid in the field. When the beginning of the month came, the king went in to the table to eat.
The king sat on his seat as he usually did, on the seat beside the wall. Jonathan sat in front of him on the right, and Abner sat on the king’s left. But he noticed David’s seat.
Saul said nothing that day, for he said, “Perhaps some defilement has happened to him. He is still unclean and has not yet purified himself.”
The next day, on the second day of the month, they noticed David’s place. Saul said to his son Jonathan, “Why has Jesse’s son not come, either yesterday or today, to sit at the table and eat?”
Jonathan answered Saul, saying, “David asked me to let him go up to Bethlehem, his city.

He said to me, ‘Let me go today, because there will be a sacrifice for the clan in the city, and my brothers have given me instructions about it. So now, if I have found favor with you, I will arrange to go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not sat at the king’s table.”

Saul became very angry with Jonathan and said to him, “You son of women who have been cast out! Don’t I know that you are a friend of Jesse’s son, to your own shame and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?”
For as long as Jesse’s son remains alive on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. So now send for them to bring the young man, because he deserves to die.
Jonathan answered his father, saying, “Why should he die? What sin has he committed?”
Saul raised his spear to throw it at Jonathan and kill him. Jonathan realized that his father’s evil resolve to kill David was settled.

Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger. He did not sit down to eat bread with his father that day, the second day of the month, because he was deeply grieved over David, for his father’s evil resolve against him was settled.
The next morning, Jonathan went out to the field according to the arrangement he had solemnly made with David, and a young servant was with him.
Jonathan said to the servant, “Hurry and find the arrows I have shot.” The servant ran, and Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
The servant came to the place where the arrow was, the place where Jonathan had shot it. Jonathan called out, saying, “The arrow is on that side of you, farther beyond you!”
Jonathan called out again to his servant, shouting to him, “Hurry! Bring them, and do not stop at all!” Jonathan’s servant gathered the arrows and brought them to his master.
The servant knew nothing about the matter. Only Jonathan and David knew about their agreement.
Jonathan loaded his equipment onto his servant and said to him, “Go on, and go into the city.”

When the servant had gone into the city, David got up and came out from the place where he had been. He fell facedown and bowed to him three times. They kissed each other and wept together for a long time.

Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace. In accordance with the oath we swore to each other in the Lord’s name, saying, ‘The Lord will be a witness between me and you, and between your descendants and my descendants forever,’ he will indeed remain a witness.”
David got up and went away, while Jonathan went into the city.
David went up to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech was alarmed when he came in to meet him and said to him, “Why are you traveling alone, with no one traveling with you?”

David said to the priest, “The king gave me an assignment today. He said to me, ‘Do not let anyone know about the matter for which I am sending you or about what I have entrusted to you.’ And I gave instructions to the young men at the place called ‘God’s faithful one,’ Phellanim Nemonim.”
“Now then, if you have five loaves of bread on hand, give me whatever you can find.”
The priest answered, “We have no ordinary bread on hand, only the holy bread of the Presence. If the young men have kept themselves clean from women, they may eat it.”

David answered the priest, “Yes, we have kept away from women since yesterday and for three days, when we set out on the road. All the young men have purified themselves. The journey you are speaking of is ordinary, but today it will be made holy because of my equipment.”

Ahimelech the high priest gave him the bread of the Presence, since there was no bread there except what had been placed before the Lord. This was the bread that had been removed from before him so that other bread, warm or fresh, could be put there on the day he took it.
One of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained there without freedom in his master’s presence. His name was Doeg the Edomite, and he tended Saul’s mules.
David said to Ahimelech, “See whether you have a spear or a sword here. I could not bring my sword or my equipment with me, because the assignment the king entrusted to me is very urgent.”

The priest said to him, “Here is the sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the place of Emath. It is lying here, wrapped in a cloth. If you want it, take it, for there is no other here except this one.” David said to him, “If there is no other except this one, give it to me.”
He gave it to him. David got up that day and fled from Saul, and David went to Achish, king of Gath.

The servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Is this not David, whom the women came out to meet, dancing and saying, ‘Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”
David took these words to heart and was very afraid of Achish, king of Gath.

He changed his behavior before him and kept beating his hands against the doors of the city gate. That day he acted like those who are out of their minds. He limped this way and that before them, falling down at the doors of the gate, with his saliva running over his beard.
Achish said to his servants, “Look! You can see that this man is out of his mind. Why have you brought him in to me?”
“Am I short of madmen, that you have brought this man to me to behave like this in my presence? This man will not enter my house!”
David left that place, escaped, and went up to the cave of Adullam. His brothers and his father’s household heard about it and came to him there.
Everyone who was in distress, everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was discontented gathered around him there. He became their leader, and four hundred men were with him.
David moved from there to Mizpah in the land of Moab. He said to the king of Moab, “Let my father and my mother stay with you until I see what God will do for me.”
He pleaded with the king of Moab, and he stayed with him throughout the days David spent out of his mind.
Gad the prophet said to David, “Do not stay in this district. Get up and go to the land of Judah.” David got up, traveled, and came to live in a city called Sarich.

Saul heard that David and the other men with him had been discovered. Saul was sitting on the hill under the [?] tree in Baema, with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing before him.

Saul said to his servants standing before him, “Listen, sons of Benjamin! Will the son of Jesse really give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds?”

For all of you are deceiving me. None of you told me when my son made a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you feels sorry for me or alerts me that my son has stirred up my servant against me as an enemy, as he is today.
Then Doeg the Edomite, who was in charge of Saul’s mules, answered, saying, “I saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub, the priest.
He inquired of God through him, and he gave him bread. He also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The king sent for Ahimelech son of Ahitub and all his father’s sons, who were the priests in Nob. They all came before the king.
Saul said to him, “Listen to me, my son, son of Ahitub.” He said, “Here I am, my lord. I am listening to you. Speak.”

Saul said to him, “Why have you joined with the son of Jesse to fight against me, giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God through you, so that you could stir him up as an enemy against me, as he is today?”

The priest answered the king, saying, “Who else among all your servants is as faithful as David? He has married the king’s daughter, is commander over all his people, and is honored throughout your household.

Was it only today that I began to inquire of God for him? Do not be angry, O king, and do not let a word come from the king’s mouth against your servant or my father’s entire household. For I, your servant, know nothing of such a matter, not the smallest thing or the greatest.”
King Saul said, “You will certainly die, Ahimelech, along with your father’s household.”

The king said to those standing before him, “Attack the priests of the Lord and kill them, because they have sided with David. They knew that he was fleeing from me, but they did not tell me.” But the king’s servants were unwilling to lay their hands on the priests of the Lord to kill them.
The king said to Doeg the Edomite, “You go and kill the priests.” So Doeg the Syrian went and killed them. That day he killed three hundred and five men, all of whom wore an ephod.
He also destroyed Nob, the city of the priests, with the edge of the sword.
One son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed all the priests of the Lord.
David said to Abiathar, “I knew that day that Doeg the Syrian was there and that he would tell Saul about me. I am responsible for the lives of your father’s entire household.
Stay here with me, and do not be afraid. Wherever I seek a refuge for my life, I will also seek a place for your life, because you have fled to me.”
David was told, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah. They are plundering their threshing floors and trampling them.”
David asked the Lord, “Should we rush against the Philistines so that I can strike them?” The Lord said to David, “Go, and you will strike the Philistines and save Keilah.”
David’s men said to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judea. What will happen to us if we go down to Keilah and hand ourselves over to be plundered by the Philistines?”
David asked the Lord again, and the Lord answered him, saying, “Get up and go down to Keilah, for I will hand the Philistines over to you.”

David and his men went down to Keilah and fought against the Philistines. The Philistines fled before them. David took their livestock and struck them with a great blow. David saved those who lived in Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech went to David, he too went down to Keilah with David, with the ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had come down to Keilah. Saul said, “God has delivered him into my hands, because he has shut himself in by entering a city fortified with gates and bars.”
Saul ordered all his people to prepare for war and go down to Keilah to capture David and the men with him.
When David realized that Saul would not forget the evil he intended against him, David said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the Lord’s ephod here.”
David said, “Lord, God of Israel, your servant has indeed heard that Saul is looking for a way to come down to Keilah to destroy the city because of me.
Will they hand it over to him? And now, will Saul come down here, as your servant has heard? Lord, God of Israel, please tell your servant.”
The Lord said, “They will hand it over.”
David and his men, about four hundred men, got up and left Keilah. They traveled wherever they could go.
David stayed in the wilderness, on the mountain of Ziph, on the burning mountain, on the rugged mountain. Saul searched for him every day, but the Lord did not hand him over to him.
David learned that Saul was coming out to search for him. David was on the rugged mountain, in the new place of Ziph.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, got up and went to David at Kaine. He strengthened David’s hand in the Lord.

He said to him, “Do not be afraid. The hand of Saul my father will not reach you. Instead, you will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you, beside you. Saul my father also knows this arrangement.”
The two of them made a covenant with each other before the Lord. David stayed in Kaine, and Jonathan went home.

The men of Ziph came up from the rugged country to Saul on the hill. They said to him, “Look, David is hiding near us in Messara, in the narrow place in Kaine, on the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon, which is the mountain.
Now, then, do what your heart desires, O king. Let the king get up and come with us, for we, your servants, undertake to hand him over to the king.”
Saul said to them, “May you be blessed by the Lord, because you have shown concern for me.
Go, then, pay attention, and quickly find out again where his foot is planted—the place you told me about—lest he use some deception again.
Look, then, and find out, and I will come with you. If he is in the land, I will search for him throughout all the districts of the people of Judah.”
The men of Ziph got up and went out ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the resting place south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to pursue him. David was told, and he got up and went down to the rock in the wilderness of Maon. Saul heard, got up, and pursued David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul and his men were on the side of the mountain, and David and his men were also on the side of the mountain. God was watching over David so that he would escape from Saul. Saul and his men spread out around David and his men to capture them.
A messenger came to Saul and said, “Get up and come quickly, because the Philistines have risen against our land.”
Saul turned back from pursuing David and went to confront the Philistines. That is why they called that place “The Rock That Divided.”
David went up from there and stayed in the narrow places in En-gedi.
When Saul returned from confronting the Philistines, he received word: “Look, David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.”
He took with him three thousand men chosen from all Israel and went to search for David and the men with him in the land of Saddaim, that is, the place for trapping wild goats.
He came to the sheepfolds along the road. There was a cave there, and Saul went into it to relieve himself. David and his men were sitting on the right side of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Look, this is the day the Lord spoke to you about, saying, ‘Look, I will deliver your enemy into your hands, and you may do to him whatever seems good to you.’” David got up and cut off the edge of Saul’s robe without Saul knowing.
After this, David’s conscience troubled him because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.
David said to his men, “May the Lord never allow me to do this thing to the lord, the Lord’s anointed.”
David persuaded his men with these words and did not allow them to rise up and kill Saul. Saul got up and went out on his way.
David came out of the cave after him. David called out behind Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” Saul turned around, and David fell facedown on the ground and bowed before him.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the words of the people who tell you, ‘Look, David is seeking your life to take it’?

Look, today your own eyes have seen how the Lord delivered you into my hand today in the cave. I did not want to kill you, but I spared you, saying, ‘I will not lay my hand on my lord, because the Lord has anointed him.’

Look, the edge of your cloak is in my hands. I took it, but I did not kill you. Understand, then, and see today that there is no malice or deceit in me toward you, nor am I rebelling against you. I have not sinned against you, but you are pursuing my life to take it.
May the Lord judge between you and me, and may the Lord avenge me on you. But my hand will not be against you.
As the ancient proverb says, ‘Sin comes from the lawless.’ But my hand will not be against you.”
“Now, you king of Israel, whom are you looking for? What sort of thing are you pursuing? You are pursuing a dead dog and chasing a single flea.”
“May the Lord be judge and arbiter between me and you. May the Lord look, judge my case, and take his seat with you.”
When David finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said to him, “Is that your voice, my son David?” Saul raised his voice and wept.
He said to David, “You are more righteous than I am, my son, because you have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil.
Today you have also shown me the good you have done for me: when the Lord delivered me into your hands, you did not rise up to kill me.
If someone finds his enemy in distress and lets him go safely on his way, the Lord will repay him with good, just as you have done good today.
Now, look, I know that you will indeed reign as king, and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands.
Now swear to me by the Lord that you will not wipe out my descendants after me, and that you will not destroy my name from my father’s household.”
David swore an oath to Saul. Saul went up to his own place, and David and his men went up to Messara, the fortified place.
Samuel died, and all Israel gathered around him and mourned for him. They buried him at his home in Ramathaim. David went down to the wilderness of Maon.
There was a man in Maon whose flocks of sheep were in Carmel. That man was very rich: he had three thousand sheep and three thousand goats. His sheep were about to be sheared in Carmel.
The man’s name was Nabal, and his wife’s name was Abigail. The woman was sensible and very beautiful, but her husband was harsh and evil in his dealings. The man was a barking dog.
David heard in the wilderness that Nabal of Carmel was having his sheep sheared.
David sent ten of his servants, saying to his young men, “Go up to Carmel and go to Nabal. Greet him peacefully in my name,
saying to him, ‘May you not [?]. May you return to this day next year in these circumstances, with you well, your whole household well, and everything you own well.’
Now, look, I have heard that your sheep are being sheared. They were with us in the wilderness, and we did not trouble them in any way or drive them away during all the days they were near us.

If so, ask your servants, and they will tell you about these things. Now let your servants—that is, us—find favor with you, for we have come to you on a good day. Let your hand give your son David whatever it finds.
David’s servants spoke these words to Nabal in David’s name. But Nabal [?].
He answered David’s servants, saying, “Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse? Nowadays servants have become numerous who run away, each one from his master.
Am I to take my bread, my wine, and the meat I slaughtered for those shearing my sheep, and give them to people whose origin I do not know? I will not give them anything.”
David’s servants went back along their way to David and reported all these words to him.
David said to his men, “Let each of you strap on his sword.” Four hundred men got up and followed David, while the other hundred men stayed with the equipment.
One of her servants told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, saying to her, “Look, David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he would not answer them.
The men were very good to us. They did not drive us away at all, nor did they trouble us anywhere during all the days we were near them in the fields.
They surrounded us like walls, by night and by day, in the fields while we were tending the sheep.
Now pay attention and see what you will do, because disaster has been determined against our master and his household. He is such a worthless man that there is no way to speak with him.”

Abigail hurried and took a hundred loaves of bread, two jars of wine, five sheep that had been cooked, five measures of roasted grain, five measures of raisins, and a hundred prepared date cakes. She loaded them onto the donkeys.
She said to her servants, “Go ahead of me. Look, I am following you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal about this plan.
She was riding her donkey and coming down along the side of the mountain. David and his men were coming toward her, and she met him.

David was saying, “Perhaps I committed a sin by guarding everything he had in the wilderness, without asking him for anything from all his possessions. And on top of this, he has repaid me with evil instead of good.
May God do these things to David’s enemies, and add still more to them, if by morning I leave behind anyone belonging to Nabal who urinates against a wall.”
Abigail saw David and immediately hurried down from the donkey. She fell on her face before David and bowed to him on the ground.
At his feet she said to him, “My lord, let the wrongdoing be on me. Let your servant speak in your hearing, and listen to your servant’s words.

Do not let my lord set his heart on the heart of this worthless man. His foolishness accords with his name, which is Nabal. His name is Nabal, in keeping with the foolishness that is with him. And I, your servant, truly did not see my lord’s servants whom you sent.

Now, my lord, as the Lord lives and as you live, the Lord has not allowed you to shed blood, but has kept your hand pure. Now, my lord, may your enemies and those seeking to harm my lord become like Nabal.
Now accept this gift that your servant has brought to my lord, and give these things to your servants who stand before my lord.
Forgive your servant’s wrongdoing, for the Lord will certainly establish a secure household for my lord, because the Lord will fight my lord’s war, and no evil will be found in you.

And if someone rises up to pursue you and seek your life, my lord's life will be bound in the bundle of life with the Lord God. But he will bind the lives of your enemies in the middle of a sling and fling them away.
And the Lord will do for my lord all the good things that he said would come upon you, and he will appoint you to be ruler over Israel.

And this will not be a cause of revulsion for you or a stumbling block in my lord's heart: shedding innocent blood for nothing. My lord's hand will remain clean for him. And the Lord will do good to my lord, and you will remember your servant and do good to her.
David said to Abigail, “Baruch—that is, ‘Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel’—who sent you today to come to meet me.
And blessed is your conduct, and blessed are you, who did not let me shed innocent blood today and kept my hand from being defiled.

And as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, who prevented me today from doing you harm, if you had not risen quickly to come to meet me, not one of all those belonging to Nabal who urinates against a wall would have been left by morning.”
And David received from her all the things she had brought him, and he said to her, “Go up to your house in peace. Look, I have listened to your voice and received you favorably.”

But Abigail went to Nabal, and there he was, holding a feast in his house like a king's feast. Nabal's heart was cheerful, and he was very drunk. Abigail did not say anything at all to him until the morning light dawned.
When morning came, he had sobered up from the wine, and his wife told him these things. When he heard them, his heart sank within him, and he became rigid, like stone.
After ten days, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard, he said, “Blessed is the Lord, who has judged my case concerning the insult I received from Nabal, and rescued his servant from evil deeds. The Lord has brought Nabal's wickedness back upon his own head.” And David sent word concerning Abigail, that she should become his wife.
And David's servants came to Abigail the Carmelite and spoke with her, saying, “David sent us to you to take you as his wife.”
She rose, bowed down to the ground, and paid homage, saying, “Here is your servant, ready to serve you and wash the feet of your servants.”
Immediately Abigail mounted her donkey, and five of her female servants followed her. She followed David's servants and became his wife.
David also took Ahinoam, who was from Israel, as his wife, and both women were his wives.
But Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti, the son of Amis, who was from Ramah, to become his wife.
The Ziphites came from the scorched land to Saul on the hill and said to him, “Look, David is hiding on the hill in Chedmath, opposite Jeshimon.”
Saul rose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph, with three thousand men chosen from Israel, to search for David in the wilderness of Ziph.
And Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon, beside the road. David was staying in the wilderness, and when David saw that Saul had come down against him in the wilderness,
David sent scouts and learned that Saul had come from Keilah, prepared.

David rose before anyone knew and slipped into the place where Saul was sleeping. Abner son of Ner, the commander of his army, was there. Saul was sleeping in the wagon, and the troops were spread out around him.
David spoke to Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, saying to them, “Who will come with me into the camp to Saul?” Abishai said to him, “I will come with you.”

David and Abishai went in among the troops at night. There was Saul, lying asleep in a covered wagon, with his spear stuck in the ground beside his head. Abner and his troops were lying asleep around him.
Abishai said to David, “The Lord has delivered your enemy into your hands today. Now I will go and strike him with my spear and pin him to the ground. I will strike him just once.”
David said to Abishai, “Do not kill him. Who can lay a hand on the Lord’s anointed and escape unharmed?”
David also said, “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord disciplines him, his day will come and he will die, or he will go out to battle and be struck down with the others.”
“But may the Lord never let me lay a hand on the Lord’s anointed. Now take the spear beside his head and the water jar, and let us go back to our place.”

When David had taken Saul’s spear and the water jar beside his head, they got up and left. No one saw them, and no one knew or woke up. Instead, they were all asleep, because a terror from the Lord had fallen upon them.
David crossed over to the other side and stood on the top of the mountain, with a great distance between them.
David called out to the troops and spoke to Abner, saying, “Will you not answer me, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you, calling out to me?”
David said to Abner, “Are you not a mighty man? Who else is like you in Israel? Why, then, are you not guarding your lord the king? Someone from my troops went in to kill your lord the king.”

“What you have done is not good. As the Lord lives, you deserve death, because you have not guarded your lord the king, who is the Lord’s anointed. Now look carefully and see where the king’s spear is, and the water jar that lay beside his head.”
Saul recognized David’s voice and said, “Is that your voice, my son David?” David said, “It is I, your servant, my lord the king.”
He also said, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant like this? What sin have I committed? What wrongdoing have they found in me, or what evil?”

“Now let my lord the king listen to his servant’s words. If it is God who is stirring you up against me, may he smell your sacrifice as a sweet fragrance. But if human beings are doing these things, may they be cursed before the Lord, because they have driven me out today, preventing me from being established in the Lord’s inheritance, saying to me, ‘Go and serve other gods.’”
“Now may my blood not be shed on the ground before the Lord, for the king of Israel has set out to seek my life, though I am like a single flea, just as a partridge flees in the mountains.”

Saul said to him, “I have sinned. Go, my son David, for I will not harm you again, because my life was precious to you today. I have acted like a worthless person and have shown very great ignorance.”
David answered, “Here is the king’s spear. Let one of your servants come and take it.”
“The Lord will repay each person for his righteousness and faithfulness, just as the Lord delivered you into my hands today, and I was unwilling to lay a hand on the Lord’s anointed.”
“Just as your life was highly valued by me today, so may my life also be highly valued before the Lord. May he protect me and rescue me from every affliction.”
Saul said to David, “You are blessed, my son. You will surely accomplish great deeds and surely prevail.” David went on his way, and Saul returned to his own place.

David said to himself, “Now perhaps one day I will fall into Saul’s hands. Nothing good will happen to me unless I get up and go to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will withdraw from me and stop searching for me throughout all the territories of Israel, and I will escape from his hands.”
David got up with the four hundred men who were with him and went to Achish son of Ammach, king of Gath.
He settled with Achish in Gath, together with his men, each with his household. David was with his two wives, Ahinoam the Israelite and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.
Saul was told that David had fled to Gath, so he no longer continued pursuing him.

David said to Achish, “If I, your servant, have found favor with you, let them give me a place to live in one of the towns near the countryside, so that I may stay there. Let your servant stop living in a city where you are king.”
That day he gave him Ziklag. That is why Ziklag belongs to the king of Judah to this day.
The time David spent in the countryside of the Philistines amounted to four months.

David and his men used to go up and attack all the Geshurites and the Amalekites. The land was inhabited from Gelampsur; these were the places allotted to them, where they were established as far as Egypt.
He devastated the land, sparing neither man nor woman. He took flocks of sheep, cattle, sheep, camels, and clothing. Then they returned and came to Achish.

Achish said to David, “Whom did you go against today?” David told him, “We went against the southern region of Judah, against the southern region of Jesmega, and against the southern region of the Kenizzites.”

“We did not keep any man or woman alive to bring them into Gath. I said, ‘They must not say anything about me in Gath, saying, “These are the things David does.”’” This was his practice throughout all the days David spent in the countryside of the Philistines.
Achish placed great trust in David, saying, “He has thoroughly disgraced himself among his people Israel, and he will be my servant forever.”

In those days the Philistines gathered their forces according to their divisions to wage war against Israel. Achish said to David, “You must understand clearly that you and your men will go out with me to battle.”
David said to Achish, “That is how you will now find out what your servant will do.” Achish said to David, “Then I will make you the chief of my bodyguard for all time.”
Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned him. They buried him in Ramathaim, his city. Saul had killed the mediums—that is, those who summon the dead—and the diviners in the land.
The Philistines gathered, came, and encamped at Shunem. Saul also gathered with all Israel at Gilboa.
Saul saw the entire army of the Philistines and was afraid. His heart was deeply shaken.
Saul inquired of the Lord, but he did not answer him through dreams, signs, or prophets.
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so that I can go to her and consult her.” His servants told him, “There is a woman who is a medium in Endor.”

Saul disguised himself and put on different clothes. He went with two other men, and they came to the woman at night. He said to her, “Consult for me by the means you use, and bring up for me the person I name to you.”
The woman said to him, “You yourself know what Saul has done, how he has removed the mediums and diviners from the land. Why, then, are you laying a trap for my life to kill me?”
Saul swore to her by God, saying, “As the Lord lives, no punishment will come upon you for this matter.”
The woman said to him, “Whom do you want me to bring up for you?” He said to her, “Bring Samuel up for me.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she immediately cried out in a loud voice. The woman said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king said to her, “Do not be afraid. Tell me whom you saw.” The woman said to Saul, “I saw gods coming up out of the earth.”

Saul said to her, “What did you make out?” She said, “I see a man of light coming up out of the earth, and he is wrapped in a cloak.” Immediately Saul realized that it was Samuel. He fell facedown on the ground and bowed before him.

Samuel said to him, “Why have you disturbed me by making me come up?” Saul said to him, “Because I am in great distress. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has withdrawn from me. He no longer turns to listen to me, either through the prophets or through dreams. That is why I have now called you, so that you may instruct me about what I should do.”
Samuel said to him, “Why are you asking me, when the Lord has withdrawn from you and has sided with your neighbor?
The Lord has done to you just as he said through me. The Lord will tear your kingdom away from you and give it to your neighbor, who is better than you—David.
Because you did not obey the Lord’s voice and did not carry out his fierce anger against Amalek, the Lord has done this to you today.

The Lord will hand Israel over with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons who are with you will fall in battle. The Lord will also hand Israel’s army over into the hands of the Philistines.”
Immediately Saul lost heart and fell full length on the ground. He was terrified by Samuel’s words, and his strength failed him, for he had eaten no food that day or that night.

The woman, the medium, came in to Saul. When she saw that he was deeply shaken, she said to him, “Look, I, your servant, have obeyed your voice. I put my life in my hands and obeyed the words you spoke to me.
Now you, in turn, listen to your servant’s voice. Let me set a morsel of bread before you, and eat, so that you will have strength when you set out on your journey.”
He did not want to eat, but his servants and the woman urged him, and he listened to them. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a suckling calf in her house, and she slaughtered it immediately. She took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened loaves.
She brought them and set them before Saul and his servants. They ate, then got up and left that night.
The Philistines gathered their armies at Aphek, while Israel took up its position at Endor, which is in the land of Israel.
The Philistine rulers were marching in groups of hundreds and thousands, while David and his men were marching at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine rulers said, “Who are these people marching along with us?” Achish said to the Philistine leaders, “This is David, the servant of Saul, the king of Israel. He has stayed with us all this time; this is his second year. I have found nothing against him from the day he came over to me until today.”

The Philistine leaders were angry with him and said to him, “Send this man back. Let him return to his place, the place where you stationed him. He must not go out with us into battle, so that he does not become a conspirator or a deceiver within the army. For how could he reconcile himself to his master except with the heads of those men?
Is this not David, before whom the dancers marched, saying, ‘Saul struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

Achish called David and said to him, “As the Lord lives, you are upright and good in my sight. Your going out and coming in with me in the camp has been good, and I have found nothing evil in you from the day you came to me until today. But the rulers are not pleased with you.”
“Now turn back and go in peace, and do nothing wrong in the sight of the rulers of the Philistines.”

David said to Achish, “What sin have I committed against you? What have you found against your servant from the day I came before you until today, that I should not go out and fight the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered David, saying, “I know that you are good in my eyes, but the Philistine leaders say, ‘He must not go out with us to war.’”

“Now get up early in the morning, you and the servants of your lord who came with you. Get up early and go to the place where I settled you. Do not let your heart dwell on anything evil, for you are good in my sight. So get up early, and when the road is clear before you, go.”
David and his men got up early to leave and to guard the land of the Philistines. The Philistines went up to fight Israel.
When David and his men entered Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had attacked the southern region and Ziklag. They had struck Ziklag and burned it with fire.
As for the women and everyone in it, from the smallest to the greatest, they had killed neither man nor woman, but had taken them captive and gone on their way.
David and his men came to the city, and there it was, burned with fire. Their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
David and his men raised their voices and wept until they no longer had the strength to weep.
David’s two wives had also been taken captive: Ahinoam the Israelite and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite.

David was deeply distressed because the people spoke of stoning him. All the people were very bitter in heart, each over his sons and each over his daughter. But David found strength in the Lord his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring the ephod here.”

David consulted the Lord, saying, “Do you want me to pursue this raiding band, and will I capture it?” The Lord said to him, “Pursue it, for you will certainly catch it, and you will certainly rescue those they carried away from their hands.”
David and the four hundred men with him set out and traveled as far as the Besor stream. The remaining men stayed behind.
The four hundred men traveled with David, while the two hundred men stayed at the Besor stream.
They found an Egyptian man in the countryside, seized him, and brought him before David. They gave him bread, and he ate, and they gave him water to drink.
They also gave him a portion of food. He ate it, and his strength returned, for he had gone three days and three nights without eating bread or drinking water.
David said to him, “Whose man are you, and where are you from?” He said, “I am a young Egyptian, the slave of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me because I fell ill three days ago.”
“We went to the southern region of the Cherethites, against the roads of Judea, and against the southern region of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire.”
David said to him, “Can you lead me to this raiding band?” The servant said to him, “Swear by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master, and I will lead you to this raiding band.”

He brought me to that place, and there they were, spread out over the whole land, eating and drinking and rejoicing over all the plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.
David rushed upon them and struck them down from morning until evening and on the following day. Not one of them escaped except four hundred young men who mounted camels and fled.
David recovered everyone whom the Amalekites had carried away, and he brought back his two wives.

He left none of them behind, from the smallest to the greatest, nor anything from all the plunder, including their sons and daughters and everything that had been carried away. David brought everything back.
David took all their sheep and cattle, and they drove them ahead of the plunder. People used to say of that plunder, “This is David’s plunder.”

David came to the two hundred men who had been unable to follow him and whom he had left sitting at the Beana ravine. They came out to meet David and the people with him. David approached the people and spoke peacefully with them.

Every wicked and worthless man among the fighting men who had gone out with David answered, saying, “Because they did not go out with us, we will not give them any of the plunder we took. Instead, let each man take his wife and children, and let them get up and leave.”

David said to them, “You must not treat these men in this way, after the Lord has given these things into our hands and protected us, and has given into our hands this raiding band, or this multitude, that came against us.

And who will listen to these words of yours? These men are not inferior to you. The share of those who stayed with the equipment will be the same as the share of the one who went out to battle. We will divide it among them according to this rule.”
This rule became a command and an ordinance in Israel, continuing to this day.
David went up to Ziklag and sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah and to all the others close to him, saying to them, “Look, I have sent you a gift from the plunder of the Lord’s enemies.”
Those in Beth-zur, those in Ramah in the south, and those in Jattir.
And to those in Aroer, those in Ammadi, those in Saphi, and those in Esthie;
and to those in Carmel, those in the cities of Israel, and those in the cities of the Kenizzites;

The Philistines fought against Israel. The men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines surrounded Saul and his sons, and the Philistines killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul’s sons.
The battle grew fierce around Saul. The archers found him, shot at him, and wounded him in the diaphragm.

Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and stab me with it, so that these uncircumcised men do not come and kill me and mock me.” But his armor-bearer was unwilling to kill him, because he was very afraid. So Saul took his sword and threw himself on it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul had died, he too threw himself on his sword and died with him.
Saul died, along with his three sons and his armor-bearer, and all the other men with him died that day.

When the men of Israel on the other side of the valley and on the other side of the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and fled as well. The Philistines came and settled in them.
The next day, the Philistines came to strip the dead. They found Saul and his three sons lying slain on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped him of his armor. They sent word throughout the surrounding area and the land of the Philistines, proclaiming the news to their idols and their people.
They placed his armor in their temple of idols and fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.
The inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul.
All the brave men got up and traveled all night. They took Saul’s body and the body of his son Jonathan from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them up to Jabesh, and burned them there.
They buried them under the [?] in Jabesh and fasted for seven days.
